query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: Under high-temperature, cyclic loading conditions, an initially single‐phase high-entropy alloy undergoes stress‐assisted microsegregation that locally enhances the formation of nano-scale brittle precipitates at grain boundaries, thereby triggering a transition from ductile to brittle fracture behavior.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast, uniformly mixed single-phase compositionally complex high-entropy alloy with minimal grain-boundary segregation and no secondary phase precipitation.
generation.intervention: Apply controlled thermal ageing combined with cyclic mechanical loading to simulate service conditions that promote diffusion and potential segregation.
generation.conditions: Experiments should be conducted at elevated temperatures and under cyclic loading regimes typical of demanding engineering service conditions, which accelerate atomic diffusion and stress-driven segregation.
generation.structural_mediator: Nano-scale precipitates at grain boundaries formed via localized compositional fluctuations induced by stress-assisted microsegregation.
generation.mechanism: The combined effects of thermal activation and cyclic stress enhance the mobility of minor constituents, leading to nonuniform partitioning at grain boundaries. This local enrichment promotes the nucleation of brittle, nano-scale precipitates, thus undermining the grain-boundary cohesion that is critical for toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples exposed to the intervention conditions will show measurable toughness degradation with a shift from ductile to brittle fracture characteristics. Electron microscopy (e.g., TEM or atom probe tomography) would reveal the presence of nano-scale precipitates along the grain boundaries, which are absent in the as-cast baseline specimens.
generation.baseline: The initial, uniformly microstructured single-phase alloy, which exhibits high toughness and ductile fracture behavior in the absence of high-temperature cyclic loading.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to dominate only under service conditions that involve sustained high temperature and cyclic loading. Under lower temperature or static loading conditions, the alloy is predicted to maintain its homogeneous microstructure and toughness.
generation.uncertainty: The precise temperature and stress thresholds needed to initiate significant microsegregation and precipitate formation remain undetermined and may depend on subtle compositional variations.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy samples: one set subjected to the combined high-temperature ageing and cyclic loading conditions; a control set maintained at lower temperature with static loading. Post-intervention, perform detailed microstructural analyses and mechanical toughness tests on both sets.
measurements: Electron microscopy (TEM/SEM) to identify and characterize any grain-boundary precipitates.
Atom probe tomography or energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) for chemical segregation analysis.
Fracture toughness and bending tests to quantitatively assess mechanical behavior changes.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples subjected to high-temperature cyclic loading do not exhibit the formation of nano-scale precipitates at grain boundaries or if they maintain ductile fracture behavior and similar toughness as the control samples, then the hypothesis that stress-assisted microsegregation leads to brittle behavior in high-entropy alloys is falsified.
